summary:
Same-sex conduct has been legal since the Penal Code entered into force in November 2012, and the age of consent is set equally regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. The sources disagree on the figure: two record it at 16, while a third states that Law 15/2021 raised it to 18 for everyone in 2021. Travellers should treat 18 as the operative figure until confirmed, since the higher number, if correct, applies to visitors as well as residents.

São Tomé and Príncipe has no legal framework for gender-identity recognition. There is no procedure for amending sex or gender markers on identity documents, so a traveller whose passport, visa or other papers do not match their presentation should expect that mismatch to be visible to border and hotel officials with no domestic remedy behind it.

No form of relationship recognition exists for same-sex couples. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised, so a foreign partner arriving on a spouse-derived entitlement has no locally recognised status to rely on.

Crimes motivated by sexual-orientation hatred attract enhanced sentencing under Article 130(2)(d) of the Penal Code, which places sexual-orientation-motivated offending above the ordinary sentencing range. The inventory does not record equivalent treatment for gender-identity-motivated crimes.

The Labour Code of 2019, Article 16.2, bans workplace discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and that is the only codified anti-discrimination protection in the sources; no general protection across housing, services or public accommodation is recorded. São Tomé and Príncipe is listed among the signatories to an international joint statement on sexual orientation and gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
The country has no states, provinces or territories with separate legal systems: the Penal Code, the Labour Code and the Civil Code apply uniformly across the national territory, so there is no sub-national variation in what a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor will encounter.

A 2016 poll found that 46 per cent of São Toméans would not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour. That measure covers LGB visibility rather than gender identity specifically, and it predates Law 15/2021 by five years, so it indicates a divided rather than hostile public baseline rather than a safety guarantee.

The absence of a gender-recognition procedure contrasts with the workplace and hate-crime protections on the books: documentation rules and substantive criminal-law protections have developed separately, and neither fills the gap left by the other.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, which affects national identity cards, civil registration, and the records used for employment, banking and healthcare. A resident changing presentation in everyday life has no document that can be brought into line.

Same-sex couples cannot marry, register a civil union or enter a domestic partnership, and the sources record no adoption available to same-sex couples. Succession, next-of-kin and inheritance questions therefore fall back on default statutory rules.

The workplace protection in Article 16.2 of the Labour Code 2019 is available to employees, and Article 130(2)(d) of the Penal Code allows a court to enhance a sentence where a crime was motivated by hatred of the victim's sexual orientation. Outside employment, no general statutory ban on discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is recorded in the sources.
outOfScopeNotes:
The current age of consent is unresolved: one source records 16 under the 2012 Penal Code and another records 18 following Law 15/2021, and the inventory contains no text of either provision to settle which is in force. Visitors should verify the figure against the current statute before relying on it.

Whether the enhanced-sentencing provision in Penal Code Article 130(2)(d) has ever been applied in practice, and whether it extends to offences motivated by gender identity rather than sexual orientation, is not sourced here. No enforcement statistics, complaint procedures or case outcomes are available in the inventory.

The sources record no information on prison or detention conditions, border-screening practices, or the treatment of gender-nonconforming travellers during security checks in São Tomé and Príncipe. Nothing is stated either way about availability of gender-affirming healthcare or HIV services for visitors.
